questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Summary
questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Understanding patterns and listening carefully help Jonah handle an unexpected problem.
choices.B: Musicians should always memorize every page before performing.
choices.C: An old piano prevents Jonah and Elise from playing well together.
choices.D: The program director wants the cousins to skip their recital.

questions.correctAnswer: Understanding patterns and listening carefully help Jonah handle an unexpected problem.
questions.explanation: Jonah uses musical structure and attentive listening to perform successfully without the missing page.
questions.stimulusText:
For weeks, Jonah had practiced a short piano duet with his cousin Elise. At the community recital, they would play on the hall’s old upright piano, whose keys felt heavier than those on Jonah’s keyboard at home. He worried about the quick final section, so he practiced it until his hands could nearly move without thought.
Just before the recital, Elise opened the music and discovered that the last page was missing. Jonah searched their folders, the bench, and even beneath the piano. The audience settled into its seats while the program director quietly asked whether they needed to skip their turn.
Elise shook her head. She remembered the upper part, and Jonah knew most of the lower one. Still, he could not recall two measures near the end. Then he noticed a pattern: the uncertain measures echoed an earlier phrase, but began one step lower. He traced the pattern on the silent keys and nodded.
They began. The unfamiliar weight of the keys demanded attention, yet Jonah listened closely to Elise instead of racing ahead. When they reached the missing measures, the repeated pattern guided him. Their final chord was not perfectly simultaneous, but it was strong. Backstage, Jonah found the missing page tucked inside another piece. He laughed. The page had been useful during practice, but careful listening and understanding the music had carried them through the performance.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: Why does warm surface water remain above colder water during summer?

choices.A: Warm water is less dense than cold water.
choices.B: Wind pushes all cold water to the lake bottom.
choices.C: Dissolved nutrients make surface water lighter.
choices.D: Sediment prevents the two layers from touching.

questions.correctAnswer: Warm water is less dense than cold water.
questions.explanation: The passage directly identifies the density difference as the reason warm water stays above cold water.
questions.stimulusText:
In many deep lakes, the water does not remain evenly mixed throughout the year. During summer, sunlight warms the upper layer. Because warm water is less dense than cold water, it stays near the surface. Deeper water remains cooler, and a narrow transition zone separates the two layers. Wind may stir the surface, but it usually cannot mix the entire lake.
As autumn air cools the surface, the upper water becomes denser. Eventually, its temperature approaches that of the deeper water. The density difference weakens, allowing wind to circulate water from top to bottom. This seasonal mixing is called turnover.
Turnover redistributes more than heat. During summer, tiny organisms near the surface may use dissolved nutrients, while decaying material carries nutrients toward the bottom. At the same time, deep water may receive little new oxygen from the air. When the lake mixes, oxygen moves downward and nutrients move upward.
This process can briefly make the water look cloudy because sediment and organic material are stirred. The cloudiness does not necessarily indicate pollution. In fact, turnover often supports the lake’s living community by renewing access to oxygen and nutrients. A similar mixing period may occur in spring, after ice melts and before surface water becomes much warmer than deep water.

questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Summary
questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?

choices.A: Effective maps select and simplify information according to a specific purpose.
choices.B: Subway maps are less accurate than maps used by hikers.
choices.C: Cartographers should include every landmark that can fit on a page.
choices.D: Map readers mainly need to understand how scale is calculated.

questions.correctAnswer: Effective maps select and simplify information according to a specific purpose.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that mapmakers choose and generalize details to meet users’ particular needs.
questions.stimulusTitle: The Work Behind a Useful Map
questions.stimulusText:
A map may appear to be a simple picture of a place, but every map is also a collection of decisions. A cartographer must decide what to include, what to leave out, and how to represent features that cannot all fit at their actual size.
Those decisions depend on purpose. A subway map emphasizes station order and transfer points, even if the drawn routes bend differently from the tracks beneath the city. A hiking map gives more attention to elevation, water sources, and trail junctions. A map made for emergency planning may highlight evacuation routes and shelters while omitting details that would distract from quick decisions.
Scale creates another challenge. On a neighborhood map, individual streets and buildings may be useful. On a map of an entire country, those same features would crowd the page. Cartographers therefore generalize: they simplify coastlines, combine minor roads, or select only the most relevant landmarks.
These choices do not make a carefully designed map dishonest. Instead, they remind readers to ask what job the map was designed to perform. Trouble begins when a reader expects one map to answer every possible question. The best map is not necessarily the one with the most information. It is the one whose selected information helps its intended users see the relationships they need.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What tool helps Leah check whether the letters are arranged correctly?

choices.A: A ruler beside the press
choices.B: A mirror beside the frame
choices.C: A lamp beneath the paper
choices.D: A photograph of the entrance

questions.correctAnswer: A mirror beside the frame
questions.explanation: The mirror shows how the reversed letter arrangement will appear when printed.
questions.stimulusText:
Leah volunteered to print a large welcome poster for the school language fair. The art room had a small hand press, and she arranged wooden letters in a frame exactly as the words should appear. When she lifted the first sheet, the message was backward.
Mr. Okafor did not reset the letters for her. Instead, he placed a mirror beside the frame. In the reflection, Leah could read the arrangement correctly. She realized that the raised letters touched the paper face down, so the frame had to hold a reversed version of the final message.
Leah began again, checking each line in the mirror before tightening the frame. The second proof was readable, but the spaces between words were uneven. She inserted thin blank blocks, printed another proof, and compared the margins on both sides. Each test used more paper, yet every proof revealed a different problem while it was still easy to fix.
On the morning of the fair, the finished poster hung above the entrance. Visitors saw a clean message in three languages. Leah noticed something else: the poster looked simple only because the complicated decisions had been settled before the final sheet was printed.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What do the comb-like projections on an owl feather do?

choices.A: Divide a strong air stream into smaller currents
choices.B: Hold rainwater away from the wing
choices.C: Increase the bird’s speed during long flights
choices.D: Make the feather surface harder

questions.correctAnswer: Divide a strong air stream into smaller currents
questions.explanation: The passage states that the projections split a strong stream of air into smaller currents.
questions.stimulusText:
Many birds create a noticeable rush of air as their wings move. Owls, however, can approach prey with unusually little flight noise. Their silence does not come from one feature alone. Several parts of an owl feather work together to change how air passes over the wing.
Along the front edge of a primary wing feather, small comb-like projections divide a strong stream of air into many smaller currents. A soft, velvety surface on the feather absorbs some of the tiny vibrations created by those currents. The trailing edge is fringed rather than sharply cut, which allows air to leave the wing more gradually.
These features reduce noise, but they also create trade-offs. The soft feather surface is not ideal for high-speed flight in heavy rain, and most owls do not travel as rapidly as some daytime hunters. Quiet movement is especially useful during short flights when an owl must listen for faint sounds below.
Engineers study owl feathers when designing quieter fans, turbines, and aircraft parts. A useful design does not simply copy the shape of a feather. It identifies how separated airflow, soft surfaces, and gradual edges reduce sound, then adapts those principles to a different material and purpose.

choices.D: To prove that all flight noise can be eliminated

Along the front edge of a primary wing feather, small comb-like projections divide a strong stream of air into many smaller currents. A soft, velvety surface on the feather absorbs some of the tiny vibrations created by those currents. The trailing edge is fringed rather than sharply cut, which allows air to leave the wing more gradually.
These features reduce noise, but they also create trade-offs. The soft feather surface is not ideal for high-speed flight in heavy rain, and most owls do not travel as rapidly as some daytime hunters. Quiet movement is especially useful during short flights when an owl must listen for faint sounds below.
Engineers study owl feathers when designing quieter fans, turbines, and aircraft parts. A useful design does not simply copy the shape of a feather. It identifies how separated airflow, soft surfaces, and gradual edges reduce sound, then adapts those principles to a different material and purpose.

questions.stimulusTitle: When Elevators Learned to Show Their Location
questions.stimulusText:
Early passenger elevators moved people between floors, but riders often had little information about where the car was. An operator controlled the motion and announced each stop. In a busy building, a person waiting in the hallway might not know whether the elevator was one floor away or near the roof.
As buildings grew taller, manufacturers added position indicators. Some early systems used a moving pointer beside a vertical list of floor numbers. Others placed small lamps above the doors. The elevator car activated a switch as it passed each floor, causing the matching lamp to glow.
The indicator did more than satisfy curiosity. People waiting could decide whether to remain at one elevator or walk to another. Maintenance workers could also notice when the displayed position did not match the car's actual location. Later systems added direction arrows, arrival signals, and spoken announcements.
Modern digital displays look different from the mechanical pointers of earlier buildings, but they solve the same communication problem. The machine is moving inside a closed shaft, while the people using it need clear information outside that shaft. A small display connects those two situations by making hidden motion understandable.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central lesson developed through Eli’s work on the exhibit?

choices.A: Historical exhibits should include only photographs with complete labels.
choices.B: Old business records are more reliable than family memories.

choices.D: Libraries should avoid displaying photographs from private collections.

questions.correctAnswer: Careful research and community knowledge can restore an overlooked part of history.
questions.explanation: Eli combines documentary research with information from a visitor, allowing the exhibit to identify a person whose story had been overlooked.
questions.stimulusText:
Eli volunteered to help prepare a small history exhibit for the neighborhood library. Most of the photographs already had labels, but one image showed a young woman standing beside a delivery bicycle with no name beneath it. The only clue was a penciled note on the back: “First route, 1948.”
The exhibit coordinator suggested labeling the woman as an unidentified worker. Eli hesitated. The bicycle carried the faded emblem of a bakery that had once operated two blocks away, so he searched old advertisements and city directories. He found the bakery's address but no list of employees. Next, he compared the photograph with a group picture from a street festival. One face looked similar, although the image was too blurred to be certain.
On opening day, Eli placed a temporary card beside the photograph explaining what he had learned and asking visitors to share information. An older visitor studied the image for a long time. She recognized the woman as her aunt, Celia Moreno, who had delivered bread while the bakery's regular drivers were serving overseas. The visitor returned the next morning with a letter that mentioned Celia's route.
Eli replaced the temporary card with a fuller label, including Celia's name and the source of the identification. The coordinator thanked him for refusing to make a quick guess. Eli realized that leaving a question open had not weakened the exhibit. It had invited the community to help complete the record.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is reverberation?

choices.A: A sound that is completely absorbed by soft material
choices.B: Reflected sounds that return quickly and blend with the original sound
choices.C: A vibration produced only by musical instruments
choices.D: A distinct echo heard after a long period of silence

questions.correctAnswer: Reflected sounds that return quickly and blend with the original sound
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines reverberation as reflections that return rapidly and merge with the original sound.
questions.stimulusText:
An echo occurs when sound waves strike a surface and return to a listener after a noticeable delay. In a large, empty room, hard walls, floors, and ceilings reflect much of the sound instead of absorbing it. A clap may therefore be heard more than once, or speech may seem to linger after a person stops talking.
Not every reflected sound becomes a distinct echo. In smaller rooms, reflections often return so quickly that they blend with the original sound. This blending is called reverberation. A little reverberation can make music sound rich, but too much can make words difficult to understand because one syllable overlaps the next.
Designers control reflections in several ways. Curtains, upholstered seats, carpets, and acoustic panels absorb part of a sound wave's energy. Irregular surfaces can diffuse sound, scattering it in many directions rather than sending a strong reflection toward one location. The placement of these materials matters as much as the amount used.
The goal is usually balance, not complete silence. A lecture hall needs clear speech, while a concert hall may benefit from longer reverberation. By measuring how quickly sound fades and where strong reflections occur, designers can shape a room for its intended use.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Many Jobs of a Public Square
questions.stimulusText:
Public squares have served cities for centuries, but their value does not come from one fixed design. Some began as marketplaces where farmers and craftspeople sold goods. Others formed near government buildings, places of worship, or transportation routes. Their locations made them natural meeting points.
A successful square usually provides both open space and useful edges. The center may hold a market, performance, or public ceremony. Along the sides, trees, steps, benches, and storefronts give people places to pause. These boundaries help a large space feel connected to everyday street life rather than empty or exposed.
The uses of a square can change throughout a single day. Commuters may cross it in the morning, children may play there in the afternoon, and an audience may gather for music in the evening. Designers cannot predict every activity, so movable chairs, level surfaces, shade, and access from several directions can make the space adaptable.
When a square is judged only by its appearance in a photograph, its most important quality may be missed. A public square succeeds when people can enter it easily, remain comfortably, and use it in more than one way. Its design is therefore less like a finished picture than a framework for shared life.

questions.stimulusText:
Nico was helping the stage crew raise a painted backdrop for the school play. During rehearsal, the backdrop stopped halfway up and tilted toward one side. Pulling harder only made the rope groan.

questions.stimulusTitle: How Antlion Pits Trap Moving Sand
questions.stimulusText:
An antlion larva lives beneath loose, dry sand and builds a cone-shaped pit. It begins by moving backward in a circle while flicking grains away with its head. As the circle tightens, the center becomes deeper and the sides become steep.
The slope of the finished pit is close to the steepest angle at which the sand can remain stable. When a small insect steps onto the edge, grains begin to slide. The insect tries to climb, but each movement may loosen more sand. The antlion waits below the center and sometimes throws additional grains upward, creating more small slides.
The pit does not pull an insect downward like a machine. Instead, it uses the behavior of loose grains. A shallow slope would be easier to cross, while a much steeper slope would collapse before the trap was ready. The antlion repeatedly repairs the sides so they remain near the useful angle.
Scientists study these pits to understand movement on unstable surfaces. The same principles can help explain why feet, wheels, and digging tools behave differently in sand than on solid ground. The antlion's trap is effective because its shape works with the material rather than against it.

questions.stimulusTitle: Why Translators Keep More Than One Draft
questions.stimulusText:
Translating a paragraph involves more than replacing each word with a word from another language. A sentence may contain an expression that sounds natural to one audience but confusing to another. Its rhythm may also affect whether the speaker sounds formal, playful, impatient, or calm.
For this reason, translators often prepare several drafts. One draft may stay close to the original sentence structure so that no idea is lost. A second may rearrange the wording to sound natural in the new language. A third may focus on tone, especially when the text includes humor, dialogue, or instructions.
The drafts are then compared. A smooth sentence is not successful if it changes the meaning, and a perfectly literal sentence may fail if readers cannot understand its purpose. Translators may read a passage aloud, ask another speaker to review it, or return to surrounding paragraphs for context.
The final version hides most of this comparison. Readers see one set of words, not the abandoned choices beside it. Yet those alternatives are valuable. They allow the translator to test meaning, clarity, and voice separately before selecting language that balances all three.
